New In Machine Learning (NewInML) Workshop @NeurIPS 2026

2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling

Aarya Bhave Affiliation: Google Email: aaryabhave@google.com    Anushka Ajay Bhave Affiliation: Google Email: nushiva@google.com
Abstract

Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications (≈50×{\approx}50\times GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

1 Introduction

Dense non-rigid registration is the problem of recovering a pixel-wise deformation field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} such that a moving image SbS_{b}, resampled through the field, comes into geometric agreement with a reference image SaS_{a}. Formally, one seeks

𝚽∗=arg⁡min𝚽⁡𝒟⁡(Sa,Sb∘𝚽)+λ​ℛ​(𝚽),\mathbf{\Phi}^{*}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{\Phi}}\;\mathcal{D}\!\left(S_{a},\;S_{b}\circ\mathbf{\Phi}\right)+\lambda\,\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{\Phi}), (1)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} measures structural dissimilarity and ℛ\mathcal{R} regularizes the field toward physically plausible, smooth deformations. This formulation underlies deformable medical image registration, dense correspondence estimation in natural images, and structural alignment in biology [1, 2, 3, 4]. Classical methods solve Equation 1 by iterative per-pair optimization, which is accurate but slow and sensitive to initialization. Learning-based methods amortize this optimization into a feed-forward predictor of 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} [2, 5, 6, 7], but most require supervised ground-truth deformation fields, which for real data essentially never exist and must be simulated [7, 8]. Unsupervised dense registration, which trains from image pairs alone using the similarity functional itself as the learning signal, removes this bottleneck [1]. A second, less discussed obstacle is architectural: correspondence information lives in fine image structure, yet max pooling retains only localized maximal responses and average pooling attenuates and blurs local structure [9, 10, 11], degrading the very signal a registration network must correlate.

In this work we transfer an unsupervised registration paradigm across both domain and dimensionality. The Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net) of Zeng et al. [4] aligns 3D subtomograms in cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET) without any labels, reducing alignment error by 40–50% while accelerating the overall process 70–110×\times. Its mechanism, dense symmetric correlation of deep feature maps followed by transformation regression, is largely modality-agnostic [2, 4]. We hypothesize that the same mechanism, redesigned in two dimensions, solves general 2D elastic registration. Our adaptation (Figure 1) differs from the original in two fundamental ways: all three modules are rebuilt for 2D inputs, and, more consequentially, the rigid transformation head is replaced with a Dense Spatial Transformer, which regresses a sparse control-point grid of 2​G22G^{2} local displacements lifted to a full-resolution dense field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} by bicubic interpolation. This changes the transformation class from rigid motions to a smooth, expressive family of elastic warps, keeping the field smooth by construction and the parameter count small.

We evaluate this framework on contact-based fingerprint alignment, and we argue that fingerprints are a deliberately demanding testbed for dense elastic registration rather than merely an application. First, ridge patterns are quasi-periodic and locally self-similar: sliding a patch by one ridge wavelength produces a near-perfect local match that is globally wrong, so local matching faces an extreme aperture problem and a registration network succeeds only by integrating long-range spatial context. Second, the deformations are authentic and free: elastic skin pressed and twisted against a rigid sensor produces genuine large-displacement, non-linear warps in every acquisition [12, 13, 14], on which rigid and affine models demonstrably fail. Third, the domain supplies an independent verification oracle. Registration evaluation is usually circular, since alignment quality is measured with the same class of similarity functional that was optimized. Fingerprint minutiae, by contrast, are precise point landmarks consumed by an external matching algorithm: a field that restores true structure raises genuine match scores while leaving imposter scores unchanged, whereas a field that hallucinates or folds structure is immediately penalized. Fourth, the correspondence signal is concentrated in a narrow fine-scale band (the ridge frequency), so fingerprints isolate the causal effect of information-preserving downsampling: pooling that destroys the ridge band destroys registration. Finally, procedural synthetic generators provide unlimited template–impression training pairs, leaving real benchmarks untouched for zero-shot transfer evaluation.

In summary, the primary contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    Cross-domain transfer of unsupervised registration: We transfer the Gum-Net paradigm from volumetric cryo-ET alignment to 2D elastic registration, redesigning all three modules and replacing rigid regression with a Dense Spatial Transformer that predicts a control-point-parameterized dense field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}, trained fully unsupervised, circumventing the deformation ground-truth bottleneck.

  • •

    Information-preserving spectral downsampling: We implement DCT spectral pooling as frozen-basis matrix multiplications (≈10×{\approx}10\times GPU speedup over FFT-based extraction) and ablate it against max and average pooling to isolate its causal effect on registration quality.

  • •

    Externally validated evaluation: We evaluate predicted fields with structural correlation and through an independent minutiae matcher acting as a topological-correctness oracle, showing that alignment raises genuine similarity while leaving imposter similarity unchanged.

We deliberately evaluate depth-first on a single demanding domain; downstream minutiae-matching results serve as a probe of topological correctness and genuine-score separability, not as a benchmark of a complete recognition system.

2 Related work

2.1 Dense non-rigid registration and geometric matching

Learned dense correspondence is commonly built on feature correlation and cost-volume constructions that score every spatial location of one feature map against every location of the other, from which displacement fields are regressed [2, 3]. Spatial Transformer Networks [15] established the differentiable-resampling machinery for training end-to-end through a predicted warp; our Dense Spatial Transformer extends this from parametric transformations to a control-point-parameterized dense field. In medical imaging, VoxelMorph [1] showed dense registration networks can be trained unsupervised, with an image-similarity loss plus smoothness penalty replacing deformation ground truth; in effect, classical intensity-based registration amortized into a feed-forward predictor. In the fingerprint domain, dense registration and displacement-field regression have been studied classically and with deep networks [5, 6, 7, 16], but predominantly supervised, trained on simulated or annotated distortion fields. Fully unsupervised estimation of dense non-linear deformation fields remains comparatively unexplored outside the medical domain, and is the setting this work addresses.

2.2 Elastic registration in fingerprint biometrics

Our testbed has its own registration literature. Traditional fingerprint systems are minutiae-based: ridge endings and bifurcations are matched after estimating a geometric transformation between point sets [13], typically rigid or locally affine, via Hough-style voting [17] and RANSAC refinement with local structural descriptors [18, 19]. These approaches assume near-rigid geometry and depend on reliable minutiae extraction, which degrades under distortion; since real impressions exhibit non-linear stretching and torque, elastic deformation remains a primary source of false rejections [12]. Classical elastic registration addressed this directly: Bazen and Gerez fit thin-plate splines to minutiae correspondences [12], while Ross, Dass, and Jain estimate average deformation models [20] and non-linear warps from ridge curve correspondences [21]. Modern learned pipelines such as C2CL [8] and contrastive cross-domain approaches [22] retain explicit alignment modules (e.g., TPS-based rectification), but optimize them through pretrained identity networks or supervised metric learning.

Our method is best understood as the learned, amortized analogue of this classical elastic lineage: a control-point grid lifted by smooth interpolation is structurally a free-form deformation model, a close cousin of TPS. But where classical methods solve a per-pair optimization from explicitly extracted correspondences, inheriting the fragility of the extraction step, our network amortizes the inference into a single forward pass from raw pixels, learning the correspondence function itself without supervision.

2.3 Spectral representations and pooling

Frequency-domain techniques have long served the testbed domain for enhancement, translation-invariant matching, and compact descriptors [23, 24, 25, 26, 27], but for representation or rigid alignment rather than for learning non-rigid correspondence. Separately, spectral pooling (subsampling by truncating high-frequency transform coefficients) preserves substantially more spatial information per parameter than max or average pooling, with DFT [9], DCT [11], and Hartley [10] variants. This property is not domain-specific: it is a principled alternative to spatial subsampling whenever deformation must be estimated from fine structure, which is exactly the regime our testbed maximizes.

2.4 Unsupervised learning in the testbed domain

Unsupervised learning has been explored for fingerprints through RBMs, autoencoders, and GAN-based enhancement [28, 29, 30], showing that structural priors can be learned without annotation, while deep matchers, whether CNN-based [31, 32, 33, 34] or transformer-based [35, 36], learn identity-discriminative features without explicitly modeling elastic deformation, which remains a major cause of matching errors. In contrast, we learn the deformation field itself, densely and without labels.

3 Method

Our model is shown in Figure 1. It takes two grayscale images: the reference (fixed) image SaS_{a} and the moving image SbS_{b} to be registered onto it. In our evaluation domain these are a fingerprint master template and an impression of the same finger, pairs that synthetic generators produce natively (Section 4). Weight-shared feature extractors produce feature maps vav_{a} and vbv_{b}, which a Siamese matching module converts into two correlation maps: at spatial coordinate (i,j)(i,j), ca​bc_{ab} holds the similarity between vav_{a} at (i,j)(i,j) and all features of vbv_{b}, with cb​ac_{ba} defined symmetrically. Both maps are processed by identical network branches, flattened, and concatenated to estimate the transformation parameters. The spatial transformation is realized by a dense deformation field 𝚽∈ℝH×W×2\mathbf{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 2}; however, to ensure smoothness and reduce complexity, we do not regress this field directly. Instead it is parameterized by a sparse control-point grid 𝐏∈ℝ2×G×G\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times G\times G}: for each control point PiP_{i}, i∈{1,…,G2}i\in\{1,...,G^{2}\}, the network regresses a localized translation Δ​𝐩i=(Δ​xi,Δ​yi)\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}=(\Delta x_{i},\Delta y_{i}), and the resulting 2​G22G^{2} parameters are upsampled via bicubic interpolation to the full-resolution field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}. The objective is to find the field that maximizes structural overlap between SaS_{a} and the warped Sb^S_{\hat{b}}, completely unsupervised: a soft Dice alignment loss [37] plus a smoothness regularizer (Section 3.4) is back-propagated through the differentiable warp.

3.1 Feature extraction module

Popular feature-extraction backbones such as DenseNet [38], InceptionNet [39], and ResNet [40] rely on max or average pooling, whereas spectral subsampling preserves considerably more spatial information per parameter while allowing flexible output dimensionality [9]. Two-dimensional spectral pooling can be based on the DFT [9], DCT [11], or Hartley transform [10]; among these, the DCT has recurred in fingerprint pipelines [23, 24] and, relying only on real-valued cosine functions rather than complex exponentials, produces output in the real domain ℝ\mathbb{R}.

We implement our own 2D spectral pooling layer based on the 2D Type-II DCT. Our implementation achieves a significant computational speed-up by decomposing the 2D transform into sequential 1D transforms and pre-computing the spectral transformation bases via an identity-matrix mapping. This reframes the transform as a pure General Matrix Multiply (GEMM) operation, achieving a 50×50\times speedup on CUDA devices (details in Appendix C).

Rather than evaluating the standard separable Type-II DCT summation [41] (restated in Appendix C) directly, our implementation computes the full 2D transform as a single bilinear matrix multiplication:

Y=WH​X​WW⊤Y=W_{H}\,X\,W_{W}^{\top} (2)

Here WH=𝒟1​D​(IH)W_{H}=\mathcal{D}_{1D}(I_{H}) and WW=𝒟1​D​(IW)W_{W}=\mathcal{D}_{1D}(I_{W}), where 𝒟1​D\mathcal{D}_{1D} denotes the one-dimensional Type-II DCT operator, while IH∈ℝH×HI_{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} and IW∈ℝW×WI_{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times W} denote identity matrices. The inverse of the 2D Type-II DCT is well defined as the 2D Type-III DCT [41]; thus the pooled and filtered representation in the frequency domain is transformed back to the spatial domain through the 2D Type-III DCT as the output of the layer.

The layer thus shifts dimensionality reduction into the frequency domain: the Type-II DCT concentrates the structurally significant low-frequency content into the top-left of the frequency matrix; downsampling is a simple crop to the top-left hf​r​e​q×wf​r​e​qh_{freq}\times w_{freq} block; and the Type-III DCT reconstructs the spatial feature map at a chosen ho​u​t×wo​u​th_{out}\times w_{out}. We maintain hf​r​e​q≤ho​u​th_{freq}\leq h_{out} and wf​r​e​q≤wo​u​tw_{freq}\leq w_{out}, since the converse would discard retained frequencies during the inverse transform and render the crop wasteful. In each convolutional block we use a cropping ratio hf​r​e​q/ho​u​t≈wf​r​e​q/wo​u​t≈0.85h_{freq}/h_{out}\approx w_{freq}/w_{out}\approx 0.85, avoiding the aggressive reduction of 2×22{\times}2 max or average pooling, which discards 75%75\% of the spacial samples per stage. Given an input pair Sa,Sb∈ℝ1×192×192S_{a},S_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 192\times 192}, the feature extraction module derives feature maps va,vb∈ℝ512×14×14v_{a},v_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{512\times 14\times 14}.

3.2 Siamese matching module

While matching is often treated as an independent post-processing step [42, 43, 44, 45, 3], the 2D correlation layer of [2] integrates matching information directly: acting as a normalized cross-correlation G:ℝC×H×W×ℝC×H×W→ℝ(H​W)×H×WG:\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W}\times\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{(HW)\times H\times W}, it flattens one feature map to ℝC×N\mathbb{R}^{C\times N} (N=H​WN=HW) and computes, for each spatial feature of the other map, a dot product against all NN flattened features. While effective, this breaks all spatial axes of one input while preserving the other. For precise alignment of fine, repeating structure, preserving the spatial hierarchy of both images is critical, since the reference and moving images differ fundamentally in their photometric properties. Inspired by the 3D matching approach in Gum-Net [4], we therefore propose a symmetric 2D Siamese correlation layer that computes two maps, Ca​bC_{ab} and Cb​aC_{ba}, processed in parallel.

Given the two outputs of the feature extraction module (Section 3.1), va∈ℝ512×14×14v_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{512\times 14\times 14} (reference) and vb∈ℝ512×14×14v_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{512\times 14\times 14} (moving), we obtain Ca​b,Cb​a∈ℝ196×14×14C_{ab},C_{ba}\in\mathbb{R}^{196\times 14\times 14}.

The first correlation map, Ca​bC_{ab}, preserves the spatial coordinates of vav_{a}. Each element at channel kk (where k∈{1,…,N}k\in\{1,...,N\} indexes a flattened spatial location of vbv_{b}) and spatial location (h,w)(h,w) of vav_{a} is the normalized dot product, with Cb​aC_{ba} defined symmetrically:

(Ca​b)k,h,w=⟨va:,h,w,vb:k⟩∑⟨va,vb⟩,(Cb​a)k,h,w=⟨vb:,h,w,va:k⟩∑⟨vb,va⟩(C_{ab})_{k,h,w}=\frac{\left\langle v_{a_{:,h,w}},\,v_{b_{:k}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{\sum\left\langle v_{a},\,v_{b}\right\rangle}},\qquad(C_{ba})_{k,h,w}=\frac{\left\langle v_{b_{:,h,w}},\,v_{a_{:k}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{\sum\left\langle v_{b},\,v_{a}\right\rangle}} (3)

The correlation maps Ca​b,Cb​aC_{ab},C_{ba} are fed into a pseudo-Siamese network of contiguous convolutional layers. Each map is convolved separately, then the branch outputs are concatenated and flattened to predict the dense deformation field.

3.3 Unsupervised non-linear alignment module

Unlike the original Gum-Net [4], which regresses a rigid 3D transformation suitable for macromolecular structures, our architecture predicts a dense deformation field 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}. The non-linear alignment module translates the correlation representations from Section 3.2 into a pixel-wise displacement field in two stages: control-point regression and dense flow-field generation.
Control point regression: Each correlation branch is reduced by six successive 10241024-channel valid convolutions to spatial size 2×22\times 2 and flattened to ℝ4096\mathbb{R}^{4096}; the two branches are concatenated into a joint representation vc​o​r​r∈ℝ8192v_{corr}\in\mathbb{R}^{8192} that captures the geometric consensus (full architecture in Appendix A). vc​o​r​rv_{corr} is fed into a multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers of 2000 ReLU units. The final regressor head projects an output vector d∈ℝ2​G2d\in\mathbb{R}^{2G^{2}}, where GG is the resolution of the sparse control-point grid. We reshape dd with the operator ℛ:ℝ2​G2→ℝ2×G×G\mathcal{R}:\mathbb{R}^{2G^{2}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2\times G\times G}, mapping the linear activations onto their spatial coordinates on the control-point grid to obtain Δ​𝐏=(Δ​x,Δ​y)\Delta{\mathbf{P}}=(\Delta{x},\Delta{y}).
Dense flow field generation: To generate a smooth, topology-preserving dense deformation field, we upsample the coarse control points to the input resolution (H,W)(H,W) using bicubic interpolation:

𝚽=Upsampleb​i​c​u​b​i​c​(Δ​𝐏)\mathbf{\Phi}=\text{Upsample}_{bicubic}(\Delta\mathbf{P}) (4)

where 𝚽∈ℝH×W×2\mathbf{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 2}. The final aligned image Sb^S_{\hat{b}} is generated by spatially resampling the moving image SbS_{b} according to 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}:

Sb^=Sb∘𝚽S_{\hat{b}}=S_{b}\circ\mathbf{\Phi} (5)

This parameterization is, structurally, a free-form deformation model: any field in the network’s range is a bicubic lift of a coarse lattice, so smoothness is enforced architecturally, as high-frequency or folding fields are inexpressible, and is only refined, not created, by the regularizer below. It is the learned analogue of classical spline-based elastic registration [12, 21], with correspondence extraction and per-pair optimization amortized into one forward pass.

3.4 Training objective

To quantify pixel-wise alignment between the reference SaS_{a} and the warped image Sb^S_{\hat{b}}, we use the soft Dice loss [37]. Let NN be the number of pixels in the flattened images and kk index a batch of size BB:

ℒdice=1B​∑k=1B(1−2​∑i=1NSb^,k(i)​Sa,k(i)+ϵ∑i=1NSb^,k(i)+∑i=1NSa,k(i)+ϵ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{dice}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\left(1-\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{\hat{b},k}^{(i)}S_{a,k}^{(i)}+\epsilon}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{\hat{b},k}^{(i)}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{a,k}^{(i)}+\epsilon}\right) (6)

On near-binary ridge imagery, this is directly interpretable as the fraction of structure brought into coincidence. Let VV denote the predicted control-point grid; we apply a first-order smoothness penalty

ℒsmooth=𝔼⁡[‖∇xV‖2+‖∇yV‖2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla_{x}V\right\|^{2}+\left\|\nabla_{y}V\right\|^{2}\right] (7)

and train with the combined objective

ℒtotal=ℒdice+λreg​ℒsmooth.\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{dice}}+\lambda_{\text{reg}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}. (8)

No deformation ground truth, correspondence annotation, or identity label is used at any stage.

4 Experiments

We train Gum-Net entirely on synthetic data and evaluate on synthetic as well as real-world data. Unlike [4], we perform no fine-tuning or adaptation on real-world datasets: the model is evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, so all real-data results directly measure synthetic-to-real transfer of the learned registration function.

4.1 Datasets

Real datasets.

As real-world benchmarks providing organically generated elastic deformation, we evaluate on the FVC2004 benchmark [46] (110 fingers, 8 impressions each across 4 databases) and the Tsinghua Distorted Fingerprint Dataset (320 pairs of undistorted and distorted impressions) [47]. We use FVC2004 to quantify pre-matching structural alignment improvements via the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC). Conversely, the Tsinghua dataset features severe real-world torque and complex skin distortion, and we use it exclusively to stress-test downstream minutiae matching behavior.

Simulated datasets.

We use Anguli [48], a free and open-source synthetic fingerprint generator developed at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, to generate 73,500 fingerprints: 2,100 distinct impressions per noise level per class, across five signal-to-noise ratios and all fingerprint classes of the Henry classification [49]. The generator first produces a master template image, then casts impressions from that template (Figures 7 and 8 in the appendix show the templates and corpus diversity). Anguli is a procedural generator: it synthesizes orientation fields from mathematical models of singular points and grows ridge patterns by iterative filtering [48, 50]. It is not a learned generative model fitted to real fingerprints, so synthetic training involves no real biometric data at any stage; real datasets are used strictly for evaluation. Beyond scale, this yields unlimited reference–moving training pairs with correspondence guaranteed by construction.

4.2 Training

The models are implemented in PyTorch [51]. All inputs have size 1922192^{2}, though the DCT spectral pooling layers make the input size arbitrary in principle. We train a single Gum-Net model on the entire synthetic dataset (seven fingerprint classes, five noise levels) with no labels at any level, following a curriculum [52]: training begins on the least noisy data and gradually introduces higher noise, 100 epochs per level with 14,700 examples each, concluding after 500 epochs. A control-point grid resolution G=8G=8 is used throughout, with the objective ℒtotal\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} of Equation 8.

4.3 Evaluation

Evaluation of registration quality.

To quantify the performance of the predicted dense deformation field, we measure pixel-level structural correspondence between the reference SaS_{a} and the rectified image Sb^S_{\hat{b}} using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC):

ρSa,Sb^=∑i=1N(Sa,i−S¯a)​(Sb^,i−S¯b^)∑i=1N(Sa,i−S¯a)2​∑i=1N(Sb^,i−S¯b^)2\rho_{S_{a},S_{\hat{b}}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(S_{a,i}-\bar{S}_{a})(S_{\hat{b},i}-\bar{S}_{\hat{b}})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(S_{a,i}-\bar{S}_{a})^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(S_{\hat{b},i}-\bar{S}_{\hat{b}})^{2}}} (9)

where NN is the total pixel count and S¯a\bar{S}_{a}, S¯b^\bar{S}_{\hat{b}} denote mean intensities. On near-binary ridge imagery, intensity correlation directly measures structural coincidence of ridge patterns [53, 54]; the improvement from ρ⁡(Sa,Sb)\rho(S_{a},S_{b}) to ρ⁡(Sa,Sb^)\rho(S_{a},S_{\hat{b}}) therefore evaluates unwarping capability independently of any downstream matching heuristic.

We compare against an ORB baseline [55], a feature-matching approach that strictly models linear (rigid/affine) transformations. As shown in Table 2, Gum-Net substantially outperforms ORB, achieving up to a 15.7% PCC increase on FVC2004 intra-class pairs with no real-data training. ORB in fact degrades baseline alignment on every dataset, which indicates that the deformation in these pairs lies outside the linear transformation class.

Topological validation via an independent minutiae matcher.

A registration method can inflate similarity metrics by hallucinating structure; the real question is whether the predicted field restores true topology. Our testbed supplies an external oracle for exactly this question: minutiae are precise point landmarks consumed by matchers entirely independent of our training objective, so a topology-restoring warp raises genuine match scores, a hallucinating warp is penalized, and, since no warp should manufacture similarity between different fingers, imposter scores should remain unchanged. Concretely, we evaluate with the NIST Bozorth3 [56] matcher: distorted images are unwarped via the predicted fields, minutiae are extracted from the aligned images, and matching scores form genuine and imposter distributions whose separability is summarized by the decidability index d′=|μg​e​n−μi​m​p|/12​(σg​e​n2+σi​m​p2)d^{\prime}=|\mu_{gen}-\mu_{imp}|\,/\,\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}(\sigma^{2}_{gen}+\sigma^{2}_{imp})}, where μ\mu and σ2\sigma^{2} denote the means and variances of the genuine and imposter score distributions.

As summarized in Tables 1 and 3, across both synthetic and real-world domains Gum-Net substantially increases genuine-pair scores (Δ​μg​e​n≫0\Delta\mu_{gen}\gg 0) with negligible perturbation of imposter pairs (Δ​μi​m​p≈0\Delta\mu_{imp}\approx 0), outperforming the unaligned baseline and the AP/MP variants. This asymmetry is what one would expect if the warps recover real structure: alignment increases similarity only where genuine correspondence exists, indicating that the predicted fields do not fabricate matches. These are distribution-level summaries rather than operating characteristics; full ROC/DET behavior of a complete recognition pipeline is beyond our pre-matching scope and left to future work.

Two observations deserve comment. First, on synthetic data the max- and average-pooling variants do not merely underperform; they reduce decidability relative to no alignment at all: alignment quality, not alignment presence, drives the downstream benefit, and a poorly estimated warp is worse than none. Second, on Tsinghua the average-pooling variant attains a marginally higher genuine mean than DCT (44.03 vs. 43.97), while DCT retains the best decidability. We hypothesize that Tsinghua’s enhanced, binarized impressions reduce the fine-detail advantage spectral pooling provides on raw ridge imagery; the unambiguous synthetic ordering isolates the effect on unprocessed structure. Characterizing this preprocessing–pooling interaction remains open.

5 Conclusion

We introduced 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end unsupervised framework for dense non-rigid 2D image registration, obtained by transferring the original 3D Gum-Net [4] from volumetric cryo-ET alignment to two dimensions and replacing its rigid transformation module with a Dense Spatial Transformer, so that a smooth dense deformation field is predicted without ground-truth displacement annotations while DCT spectral pooling and control-point parameterization preserve the fine structure on which correspondence depends. Trained purely on synthetic fingerprint data and evaluated zero-shot, the method improves structural correlation by 10.5% (synthetic) and up to 15.7% (FVC2004), and on Tsinghua raises genuine match scores while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged, confirming deformation quality through an external matcher rather than the training objective alone. Evaluation is restricted to a single domain by design and reports distribution-level summaries rather than operating characteristics; future work includes extending to other imagery where fine quasi-periodic structure meets elastic deformation, operational metrics on larger datasets, and coupling with fixed-length embeddings [33] for retrieval at scale.

Appendix A Detailed architecture of Gum-Net variants

To verify that DCT spectral pooling and filtering layers offer superior performance compared to max and average pooling, we built identical architectures differing only in the pooling operation, named Gum-Net MP and Gum-Net AP. Figure 4 shows the detailed architecture for Gum-Net with input size 192×192192\times 192 for both SaS_{a} and SbS_{b}; Figures 5 and 6 show the detailed architectures for Gum-Net MP and Gum-Net AP respectively. Gum-Net AP and Gum-Net MP change only the pooling within the feature extraction module (Section 3.1), keeping the rest of the architecture exactly the same.

Appendix B Dataset diversity and inference details

Figure 7 shows the master templates used by Anguli, and Figure 8 illustrates the diversity of our synthetic corpus across the seven fingerprint classes and five signal-to-noise ratios. Figure 9 shows inference plots across all finger types; the model has not seen these reference–moving pairs during training.

Appendix C Details on the DCT optimization

The 2D DCT spectral pooling layer is implemented as a sequence of frozen linear transformations to exploit highly optimized General Matrix Multiply (GEMM) routines on CUDA devices. For a 1D signal of length NN, the Type-II DCT basis matrix 𝐖∈ℝN×N\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is precomputed by applying the DCT operator to the identity matrix 𝐈N\mathbf{I}_{N}:

𝐖=DCT-II​(𝐈N)\mathbf{W}=\text{DCT-II}(\mathbf{I}_{N}) (10)

such that the transform 𝐲=𝐱𝐖⊤\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}^{\top} is equivalent to a standard 1D DCT-II applied to the row vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}. This matrix is computed once at initialization and stored as a frozen (non-trainable) weight in a linear layer, reducing repeated transform computation to a single matrix multiplication at inference time.

The 2D Type-II DCT of a feature map 𝐗∈ℝC×H×W\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} is defined as [41]

Yc,u,v=αu​αv​∑x=0H−1∑y=0W−1Xc,x,y​cos⁡(π​u​(2​x+1)2​H)​cos⁡(π​v​(2​y+1)2​W)Y_{c,u,v}=\alpha_{u}\alpha_{v}\sum_{x=0}^{H-1}\sum_{y=0}^{W-1}X_{c,x,y}\cos\left(\frac{\pi u(2x+1)}{2H}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi v(2y+1)}{2W}\right) (11)

with αu=1/H\alpha_{u}=\sqrt{1/H} for u=0u=0 and 2/H\sqrt{2/H} for u>0u>0, ∀u∈{0,…,H−1}\forall u\in\{0,...,H-1\}, and αv\alpha_{v} defined analogously. Its separability allows the transform to be decomposed into two sequential 1D operations:

𝐘=𝐖H​𝐗​𝐖W⊤\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{W}_{H}\,\mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{W}_{W}^{\top} (12)

where 𝐖H=DCT-II​(𝐈H)∈ℝH×H\mathbf{W}_{H}=\text{DCT-II}(\mathbf{I}_{H})\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} and 𝐖W=DCT-II​(𝐈W)∈ℝW×W\mathbf{W}_{W}=\text{DCT-II}(\mathbf{I}_{W})\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times W} are the precomputed basis matrices for the height and width dimensions respectively. In practice, this is computed by first applying 𝐖W\mathbf{W}_{W} along the width axis, transposing, applying 𝐖H\mathbf{W}_{H} along the (now leading) spatial axis, and transposing back, matching Equation 2 in the main paper.

Following the forward 2D DCT, a binary low-pass mask 𝐌∈{0,1}H×W\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} is applied element-wise to the frequency representation:

𝐘~=𝐘⊙𝐌,𝐌u,v={1if ​u<hfreq​ and ​v<wfreq0otherwise\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{Y}\odot\mathbf{M},\qquad\mathbf{M}_{u,v}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }u<h_{\text{freq}}\text{ and }v<w_{\text{freq}}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (13)

retaining only the top-left hfreq×wfreqh_{\text{freq}}\times w_{\text{freq}} block of low-frequency coefficients. The masked representation is then cropped to hout×wouth_{\text{out}}\times w_{\text{out}} and reconstructed via the inverse transform, where the 2D Type-III DCT (the inverse of Type-II) is applied separably using analogous precomputed basis matrices 𝐖hout−1\mathbf{W}_{h_{\text{out}}}^{-1} and 𝐖wout−1\mathbf{W}_{w_{\text{out}}}^{-1}:

𝐗^=𝐖hout−1𝐘~[:hout,:wout](𝐖wout−1)⊤\hat{\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{W}_{h_{\text{out}}}^{-1}\,\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}_{[:h_{\text{out}},:w_{\text{out}}]}\,\left(\mathbf{W}_{w_{\text{out}}}^{-1}\right)^{\top} (14)

The constraint hfreq≤houth_{\text{freq}}\leq h_{\text{out}} and wfreq≤woutw_{\text{freq}}\leq w_{\text{out}} is enforced to ensure that no retained frequency coefficients are discarded during the inverse transform, which would render the masking step computationally redundant. This GEMM-based implementation achieves approximately a 50×50\times speedup over a naive iterative DCT on CUDA devices, as matrix multiplication is among the most heavily optimized parallel primitives available on modern GPU hardware.

Figures 11 and 11 show our speedup and memory efficiency compared to a traditional implementation of the DCT in PyTorch, which uses the built-in FFT suite to extract DCT coefficients.
